I'm curious about the rationale here. Does the phrase "you get what you pay for" somehow not apply to wages? It's not necessarily true, as marketing is rarely in line with reality and prices rarely reflect actual utility of various products. Nevertheless in general you pay for higher quality goods or services, this includes workers.

At present, for most urban areas the cost of living is nearing double the current minimum wage. A simple studio apartment can run for $1200, which is over the monthly salary of a 40-hour work week for a single individual. The end result, working on barest assumptions, is the workers you end up with simply don't care about the McJob and aren't paid sufficiently to care.

This does not necessarily mean $15 an hour federal is a good idea, either. Raising the minimum wage can bankrupt local small economics in rural places, and prevent small operations from hiring employees (think Mom & Pop shop) or expanding. It further increases the disparity of wages between tipped employees and hourly, as the tip exemption (an exemption that should not exist) is still 2.13/hr and employers will punish the employees worse than they already do for not meeting $15/hr in tips.

The simple fact is that federalism is bad for local economics. Individual states may certainly set minimum wages corresponding to the costs of living to abate growing poverty and reliance on government services, but to set this as a federal wage is a terrible idea. Contrariwise, if it is not federally set this presents a severe disparity in costs of goods or services for inter-state commerce, resulting in border-hopping for goods worse than already occurs.

There does not appear to be a good solution to this problem, as in either case there are very real consequences.
